newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Interview-KTM motorcycles move in to gear on-road.
newsitem.headline: Interview-KTM motorcycles move in to gear on-road.

text.p: From a cramped plant in Upper Austria, Europe's only listed motorcycle maker KTM has established itself as a market leader off-road and is starting to chip away at foreign dominance of the highways.

Since its rescue from insolvency in 1991, KTM-Motorradholding AG has carved out a profitable niche in the European and U.S. leisure markets with "hard endurance" bikes that perform as well cross-country as they do on asphalt.
In December, the firm made its debut on the Vienna bourse with the issue of 920,000 shares at 590 schillings ($49.48) each. On Friday its shares were trading at 733.

Now chairman and shareholder Stefan Pierer is turning his attention to developing on-road motorcycles that will challenge Japanese and German manufacturers head on. And he hopes that KTM's new "mini bikes", aimed at children as young as five, will create a loyal customer base for the future.
In an interview with Reuters late on Thursday, Pierer forecast an 18 percent increase in earnings and sales in the year to August 31 and further growth in subsequent years.
"We already have almost 50 percent of our target under our belt at the half year," Pierer said.

Last year KTM's 430 workers turned out 15,000 hand-assembled motorcycles and turnover exceeded one billion schillings for the first time, rising to 1.01 billion from 812 million. Pre-tax profit reached 102 million schillings after 77 million.

The Mattighofen plant, set deep in the Upper Austrian hills, can produce up to 25,000 motorbikes a year -- a drop in the Ocean compared with the five million sold by Honda last year and the three million moved by Yamaha.
But its margins are healthy thanks to a sporty image and niche position. KTM motorcycles command a price premium of up to 25 percent over Japanese brands in some markets.

"Our strategy is the reverse of the Japanese concept. Japanese motorcycles look like endurance bikes but they are designed for the street. We come from off-road but the bikes are also good for asphalt," Pierer said.

He saw the biggest sales growth this year among mini-bikes, the Duke on-road motorcycle and a revamped line of 2-stroke racing bikes. Already in the United States KTM sells one mini-bike for every two adult motorcycles it shifts and Duke sales are expected to climb to 1,400 this year from 1,167.
Founded as a family concern in the 1930's, KTM built its early reputation on racing successes in the motocross world championships, the Dakar rally and the Isle of Man grand prix.

But failure to make commercial mileage of its race victories led to the firm's collapse in 1991. Pierer and his management team stepped in to save the Mattighofen plant and swiftly set about rethinking the firm's strategy.
"We have never forgotten our roots. We have stuck to our success off-road but we have widened our range at the top end and the bottom end," Pierer said.
"Hard endurance" motorcycles target 30 to 50-year-olds with a relatively high income and up to three motorcycles already sitting in the garage.
The firm's first on-road motorcycle, the Duke, was launched in 1994 and a second on-road bike with a two-cylinder engine is under development for an autumn unveiling.
"This time the target group will be completely different. This time we're going for the likes of Honda and BMW," Pierer said.

He said KTM was keen to take control of its own sales network. It already has majority stakes in distributors in Germany and Switzerland and has a unit in the United States. In December it bought 26 percent of Italian sales firm Farioli and is in negotiation to buy into its French representative.

In the Netherlands, KTM is close to taking a majority stake in one of its strategic suppliers, a maker of suspension components. "We have already signed a letter of intent and the deal should be sealed by the end of March," Pierer said.

Already well established in Europe and the United States, KTM is hoping for future expansion in Japan, the growing economies of Asia and Canada. The firm has also begun to branch out into the lucrative motorcycle accessories business.
"It is a first attempt for us. We are aiming for a turnover in accessories of 35-40 million schillings in the foreseeable future," Pierer said. ($ = 11.92 Austrian Schillings)
